evidence.name: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, flood hazard zones (layer 28)

limits: GloFAS models large rivers without flood defences; FEMA zones also cover small streams, ponding and, in A zones near the coast, storm surge. Much of the disagreement is a difference of scope.
FEMA zones are regulatory maps of different dates per panel; the 1 percent zone is not a depth.
The zone polygons were generalised by the service to about 1 m and 431 of 21289 are not valid polygons after that; they were rasterised as they came.
A pixel is about 90 m; a zone narrower than that can be missed.

comparisons.method: Every GloFAS pixel of the box is set against the FEMA zone that holds its centre. FEMA's 1 percent annual chance zones are the A zones (called riverine here) and the V zones (coastal); the 0.2 percent zone is zone X so labelled. GloFAS 'flooded' is a published depth at that return period on a pixel outside JRC's permanent-water layer.

evidence.name: USGS NWIS annual peaks (stage and streamflow); NOAA NWPS flood stages; USGS SIR 2018-5070, table 3

limits: A gauge stage is a height above the gauge's own datum, not a depth of water over land. Stage above the NWS flood stage is used as a rough stand-in for depth over the banks; it is not the same quantity as a GloFAS depth, which at a channel pixel includes the channel.
Whether the NWS stage scale and the USGS gage height share a datum at each gauge was not checked.
Both rivers are regulated (reservoirs upstream of Houston and Austin); the record is not stationary. A record of a few decades says little about 100 and 500 years.
The largest depth within 270 m may belong to a neighbouring channel.

map.label: Gauges and Harvey marks on the map

comparisons.method: For each stream gauge in the box: its annual peak stages, the NWS minor flood stage where NWS has the gauge, and the largest GloFAS depth within three pixels (about 270 m) of the gauge at 10, 100 and 500 years, on pixels outside JRC's permanent-water layer (where the map holds a patch value). 'Above flood stage' is a peak stage minus the minor flood stage, in metres.

evidence.name: USGS Short-Term Network, event '2017 Harvey', high-water marks in Texas

limits: Harvey was a rainfall flood: bayous, streets and reservoir pools flooded far from the large rivers GloFAS models, so a mark on a pixel that GloFAS leaves dry is expected and is not an error of the map.

How rare Harvey was differs by place: USGS SIR 2018-5070 gives annual exceedance probabilities from below 0.2 to 14 percent at 74 gauges (docs/validation/references/usgs-sir-2018-5070). It is not one return period.
A mark's height above ground is at one point; a pixel is about 90 m and its depth is over a 90 m terrain model, which in a channel includes the channel.
Marks are where surveyors went, mostly where water was; they do not sample dry places.

map.label: Gauges and Harvey marks on the map

comparisons.method: For each surveyed high-water mark with a height above ground: the GloFAS depth of the pixel that holds the mark, at 100 and 500 years. Quartiles are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles.

evidence.name: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, flood hazard zones (layer 28)

limits: GloFAS models large rivers without flood defences; FEMA zones also cover small streams, ponding and, in A zones near the coast, storm surge. Much of the disagreement is a difference of scope.
FEMA zones are regulatory maps of different dates per panel; the 1 percent zone is not a depth.
The zone polygons were generalised by the service to about 1 m and 606 of 7071 are not valid polygons after that; they were rasterised as they came.
A pixel is about 90 m; a zone narrower than that can be missed.

evidence.licence: U.S. public domain (USGS); attribution requested; peaks may be provisional
evidence.name: USGS NWIS annual peaks (stage and streamflow); NOAA NWPS flood stages; USGS SIR 2018-5070, table 3

limits: A gauge stage is a height above the gauge's own datum, not a depth of water over land. Stage above the NWS flood stage is used as a rough stand-in for depth over the banks; it is not the same quantity as a GloFAS depth, which at a channel pixel includes the channel.
Whether the NWS stage scale and the USGS gage height share a datum at each gauge was not checked.
Both rivers are regulated (reservoirs upstream of Houston and Austin); the record is not stationary. A record of a few decades says little about 100 and 500 years.
The largest depth within 270 m may belong to a neighbouring channel.

map.label: Gauges and Harvey marks on the map

comparisons.method: For each stream gauge in the box: its annual peak stages, the NWS minor flood stage where NWS has the gauge, and the largest GloFAS depth within three pixels (about 270 m) of the gauge at 10, 100 and 500 years, on pixels outside JRC's permanent-water layer (where the map holds a patch value). 'Above flood stage' is a peak stage minus the minor flood stage, in metres.
